prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: One, There, Once

outputs.L1:
I passed through; I should have paused. There were a hundred doors. One opened. In there, someone whose name is not yet known to me lived out his middle years in simple terms: two chairs, one place laid for early breakfast, one plate with dry toast and butter softening. There, his mind raced through writings he had memorized long ago while he tried to get hold of himself.

Once, in his youth, he had studied with love, in the corners of old paintings, matrices of fields and towns—passages intricate and particular: wheat, columns, figures and ground, classically proportioned in lines that were meant to meet, eventually, at vanishing point. They continued, nevertheless; they troubled the eye.

He collected sets of books printed in the nineteenth century: unyielding pages, memoirs of the poets, engravings of rurified private subjects in times of public-sector unhappiness, frescoes of human oddity in gatefold printing.

“Why does it continue to chasten me?” he says to no one. It does. It is a painful mistaking, this setting something down, saying aloud, “It is nothing yet,” when he’d meant, not anything—but then nothing peered through the keyhole; nothing took possession.

Snow on the roofs, snow in traces on the ground, passersby with wet trouser cuffs looking to the pavement as the hill rises, light gathering in the river and gradually spreading.
outputs.L2:
I went by when I ought to have stopped; around me were a hundred doors. One of them stood open. Beyond it, a man whose name I still do not know was spending the middle part of his life plainly: two chairs, a single setting for an early breakfast, one plate holding dry toast and butter beginning to soften. In that room his thoughts rushed over texts he had learned by heart many years before, as he struggled to steady himself.

When he was young, he had looked with devotion into the corners of old paintings, studying their ordered arrangements of fields and towns, their exact and complicated passages: wheat, columns, figures, background, all classically measured along lines intended, in the end, to converge at a vanishing point. Yet the lines went on; they unsettled the eye.

He gathered editions from the nineteenth century: stiff-paged volumes, lives of poets, engravings of ruralized private scenes made during eras of public misery, and foldout images portraying strange human particulars. “Why does it still go on correcting me?” he asks no one. And it does.

It is an aching error, this act of writing something down, of saying aloud, “it is nothing yet,” when what he had meant was “not anything”—only then nothing looked in through the keyhole, and nothing took control.

Snow lay across the roofs, with remnants of snow on the earth. People passed with damp trouser hems, watching the pavement as the hill climbed upward, while light collected in the river and slowly widened.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the experience of passing by countless doors, each one concealing a separate and unknown existence. Among these hidden lives, he briefly imagines or glimpses the solitary life of one particular man. This man remains largely anonymous, seen only in fragments, yet those fragments suggest a quiet and inward existence, separated from the movement and noise of the world outside.

The man’s daily life appears simple and restrained. His breakfast setting is sparse, perhaps consisting of only the most basic objects, arranged without luxury or excess. Yet this outward simplicity contrasts with the restlessness of his inner life. Though his surroundings are plain, his mind is active, uneasy, and difficult to settle. He seems to live less through action than through thought, memory, and private contemplation.

In his youth, the man had taken pleasure in studying old paintings. He looked at them with affection and attentiveness, drawn especially to their sense of order and depth. The carefully arranged perspectives, the distant roads, the small figures, and the intricate landscapes all fascinated him. These paintings offered him a world shaped by harmony and design, a world in which every detail had its place and every distance could be measured by the eye.

He also collected nineteenth-century books, volumes rich with literary memoirs, engravings, portraits, and curious images. These books preserved fragments of past lives and past imaginations. They contained records of writers, artists, eccentrics, and unusual human figures, presenting humanity in all its strangeness and variety. Through them, the man surrounded himself with traces of other minds and other eras, as if seeking companionship in the printed remains of the past.

The passage ends with the man troubled by the difficulty of expression itself. He is not merely thinking; he is struggling with how thought can be shaped into words or images. Outside, a snowy city scene unfolds, quiet and cold, adding to the atmosphere of isolation. The falling snow softens the streets and buildings, while the man remains indoors, confronted by the distance between inner experience and its outward expression.
outputs.L4:
The scene begins with the simplest of openings: a door is briefly pushed ajar, and through it we glimpse the room of an unnamed man. Nothing dramatic appears there. The room is sparse, ordinary, almost bare. Yet that small view becomes the entrance to a much larger inward landscape. The man’s solitude is not merely physical; it is mental and emotional, a state in which memory, perception, and thought press against one another without forming a stable shape. What looks at first like a plain domestic interior becomes charged with the restless movement of consciousness.

The text is concerned with memory and with the difficulty of turning experience into meaning. The man seems surrounded by fragments: impressions of snow, streets, river light, passing time, and half-formed recollections. These details do not arrange themselves into a clear story. Instead, they flicker and recede. The mind races, but its motion does not necessarily lead to understanding. The attempt to grasp life, to name it, to record it, or to preserve it in language, repeatedly threatens to fail. Words reach toward experience, but experience slips away.

This failure gives the text much of its haunting force. The ordinary world remains present: snow falls, streets lie outside, light moves on the river. Yet these familiar things feel chastening, as if they expose the limits of human interpretation. The world is visible, but not fully readable. The man can observe it, remember it, perhaps even describe it, but he cannot finally possess its meaning. In this sense, the text turns a modest scene into a meditation on the instability of consciousness and the fragility of expression.

The repeated approach toward “nothing” is especially important. “Nothing” does not simply mean emptiness or absence. It becomes the point at which thought, memory, and language break down. The more intensely the mind tries to secure experience, the more it encounters blankness. Names fail. Records fail. The self itself begins to feel uncertain. What remains is not a grand revelation, but a quiet awareness of limitation.

And yet the text is not merely bleak. Its profundity lies in the way it attends to ordinary perception. A room, a door, snow, streets, and river light become meaningful precisely because they resist easy meaning. The brief glimpse into the man’s life suggests that every consciousness contains depths that cannot be fully entered or explained. Solitude, then, is not only loneliness; it is also the condition of being inwardly unknowable, even to oneself.

By focusing on a small, almost accidental moment, the text reveals how much can be contained in a passing scene. It shows a mind struggling to make sense of memory and sensation, only to find that meaning is unstable and language incomplete. The result is a work that feels quiet but intense, ordinary but haunted, chastened by the possibility that all attempts to record experience may end in “nothing,” and yet profound in its attention to that very failure.
outputs.L5:
Once, there was one small light in the distance.

It did not shine brightly at first. It flickered quietly, almost hidden by the dark, but it was there. One traveler noticed it and followed its glow. Step by step, the light grew clearer, and the road felt less lonely.

There are moments in life when one simple thing can change everything: one choice, one word, one chance, one hope. Once we recognize it, we begin to move forward with more courage.

And sometimes, that is all we need—one reason to keep going.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, lyrical prose poem in the style of contemporary literary modernism: a narrator passes through a building with many doors and glimpses the interior life of an unknown middle-aged man, including breakfast, old books, art history, memory, and a snowy cityscape.
counterfactuals.output:
In the building of doors I entered by mistake, or was entered by, the hinges speaking softly in their brass throats, and each threshold opened not onto rooms but onto the weather of a life not mine. Behind the first door: a table at morning, the egg-cup shining like a small moon, toast cooling in a rack, coffee darkening the porcelain with its bitter astronomy. A middle-aged man sat there in a blue shirt, sleeves folded back, reading yesterday’s newspaper as if it were scripture already ruined by touch. His face had the deliberate wear of a map often refolded along the same creases. He lifted the cup; steam veiled him; he vanished into habit.

Behind another door: books, old books, their spines cracked into minor streets, their pages smelling of dust, rain, and extinguished lamps. He stood among them without reading, running one finger along titles in Latin, German, French, the dead languages of desire and discipline. Vasari, Panofsky, a catalogue of Flemish altarpieces, a monograph on the blue of Giotto’s skies. In the margins his younger hand had written urgent little verdicts—wrong, luminous, impossible—beside saints pierced by arrows, Madonnas lacquered with grief, cities no one had ever inhabited except in gold leaf. He touched these notes as one touches the pulse of a sleeping child.

A third door opened to snow. Not outdoors, not exactly, but a windowed room where the city, in its white erasure, leaned close. Roofs softened, cornices blurred, the black trees inked themselves against the park; taxis moved below like cautious beetles carrying their yellow secrets. The man watched the flakes descend with that expression peculiar to those who have remembered something before knowing what it is. Snow filled the avenues, the fire escapes, the mouths of statues, and in its slow abundance the city seemed to be forgiving itself for its noise.

Then came the door of memory, unmarked, already ajar. A girl in a red wool coat crossing a museum hall. His mother’s hand smelling of soap and onions as it turned the page of a picture book. A lecture room in winter, slide projector stuttering light onto the wall: Caravaggio’s darkness, a shoulder, a wound, the astonishment of flesh when touched by revelation. Someone laughing behind him. Someone leaving. The old humiliations kept their polish; the old tendernesses, too, retained their dangerous shine.

I passed on, though the corridor lengthened with each step, multiplying its doors like thoughts at dusk. In one room he shaved before a mirror and did not recognize the brief, stern boy inside his eyes. In another he wrote a letter and tore it up. In another he held an orange in his palm as if weighing the sun. Everywhere his life continued without needing me: breakfast becoming hunger again, books closing over their pressed flowers of thought, art offering its disciplined sorrow, the snow thickening at the glass.

At the final door I did not enter. I listened. There was only the faint sound of pages being turned, or wings, or snow settling on the city’s innumerable sills. And I understood, if understanding is permitted in such places, that every person is a building of unvisited rooms, and that to glimpse even one lit window is to be burdened forever by the rest: the locked chambers, the warm cup, the unfinished sentence, the man standing alone before a painted heaven, looking not upward but inward, where the weather had always been falling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness passage about briefly seeing into a stranger’s room and imagining his life, with themes of vanishing points, nineteenth-century books, loneliness, and the difficulty of saying “nothing.”
counterfactuals.output:
For one second—less, perhaps, because the train had already begun to slide away and the window, lit like an aquarium, was narrowing into the dark—I saw his room.

A chair first, or the idea of a chair, angled toward a small table; and on the table a green-shaded lamp making a circle of patient light, the kind of light one imagines falling on nineteenth-century books, those long-breathed volumes with marbled endpapers and moral weather, where people inherit, renounce, suffer fevers, walk across fields at dusk, and say what they mean only after three hundred pages. There were books there, certainly. Brown spines, cracked gold, a row of them leaning as if tired of standing up for history. Dickens perhaps, or Trollope, or some severe Russian who had understood the soul as a set of rooms one never quite finishes crossing.

And the man—if it was a man—stood with his back to the window.

That was all.

But “all” is a dangerous word, as dangerous as “nothing.” Nothing happened, one says. I saw nothing. It meant nothing. Yet the mind refuses such economy; it spends wildly, invents furniture in the corners, a cup cooling at his elbow, a letter folded twice and placed beneath a paperweight, a photograph turned face-down not from melodrama but from fatigue. It gives him slippers, a cough, a sister in Brighton, a dead mother, an unpaid bill, a habit of touching the top of the doorframe when entering, as though confirming that the world is still there.

The room rushed backward, or I did; the rails drew themselves together into their inevitable vanishing point, that little pinprick of certainty toward which everything straightens and disappears. How obedient perspective is, how cruel. All lines promise to meet somewhere, though one knows they never do. His life, my life, the lit window, the black glass of the train reflecting my own face over his curtains—parallel, adjacent, intimate for an instant, then flung apart.

I wanted to say I had seen into him. But I had not. I had seen wallpaper, perhaps; the yellowed square where a picture had once hung; a hand lifting to the head, or merely a shadow. And still there was the loneliness of it, not his only but mine, the loneliness of witnessing without consequence. To be outside another life is to feel how many rooms the world contains, each with its lamp, its unread book, its silence swelling after dinner.

When someone later asked what I was thinking about, I almost said, “Nothing.”

The word rose, round and blank, ready to cover everything: the window, the books, the back of his neck, the converging rails, the impossible tenderness of strangers. But it stuck. Nothing is so hard to say when something—however slight, however vanishing—has looked back at you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental prose poem with fragmented punctuation and line-break-like spacing, moving from a hallway of doors into a quiet apartment where a solitary man reflects on paintings, poets’ memoirs, engravings, and snow outside.
counterfactuals.output:
The hallway was a sentence with too many doors—

     brass numbers dimmed by thumbs  
     keyholes breathing their little dark vowels  
     paint lifting at the corners like old bandages.

He walked past each shut room as if past a possible life.  
Behind one: a radio. Behind another: water worrying the pipes.  
Behind another: laughter, cut short—  
or only the elevator swallowing itself.

His own door opened without drama.

Inside, the apartment had been waiting in its gray shirt.

     table. chair. cup.  
     the narrow lamp with its yellow doubt.  
     books stacked like weather.

He removed his coat and became, again, a solitary man,  
a figure placed carefully in a quiet interior  
by someone who preferred shadows to explanation.

On the wall: reproductions of paintings.  
A woman at a window who would never turn.  
A bowl of fruit collapsing into color.  
A saint pierced by light, unsurprised.  
He looked at them as one looks at relatives  
whose names have been forgotten but whose illnesses remain.

     blue, he thought.  
     then: no, not blue—  
     the memory of blue after evening has handled it.

On the desk lay poets’ memoirs, open and facedown,  
their spines suffering elegantly.  
Pages where hunger became doctrine,  
where love became a room with no furniture,  
where exile learned to pronounce itself  
in a borrowed alphabet.

He read a sentence. Stopped.  
Read it again for the wound beneath the grammar.

     I was young.  
     I was already leaving.  
     The city burned quietly in my pocket.

He touched an engraving beside the books:  
black lines crosshatched into a harbor,  
a horse, a condemned tree,  
clouds carved as if the sky itself were wood  
and could be cut, scored, persuaded  
to confess depth.

How patient the burin must have been.  
How certain the hand.  
To make darkness by repetition—  
line after line after line—  
until a face appeared from its own weather.

Outside, snow began its white revision.

It fell past the window without emphasis,  
covering cars, roofs, the municipal cruelty of curbs.  
The city softened into an unfinished page.  
Every footprint briefly important.  
Every sound sent back wrapped in cotton.

He stood there, cup cooling in his hand,  
and thought of all the doors in the hallway  
closed on their minor kingdoms.

     the radio.  
     the pipes.  
     the laughter.  
     the elevator descending through its iron throat.

And here: paintings that would not speak.  
Poets who had spoken too much and too late.  
Engravings dense with disciplined night.  
Snow translating the world into silence.

He wanted to write something down.

Instead he watched.

The apartment gathered around him—  
not comfort, exactly, but shape.

     lamp. chair. window. man.  
     snow.

For a moment he felt himself engraved there,  
not living, not gone,  
only held in fine black lines  
against a whiteness still falling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a melancholic literary vignette in a poetic voice: someone regrets not pausing at one of a hundred doors, behind which an unnamed man eats dry toast, recalls old studies of perspective in paintings, and watches winter light gather by a river.
counterfactuals.output:
There were a hundred doors along that corridor, each painted the color of forgotten weather, each with its brass number dimmed by the touch of hands that had gone on elsewhere. I passed them all.

At the time, I was young enough to believe that every door would open again if I wished it, that no threshold vanished simply because one did not stop before it. I walked quickly, carrying my small errand like a flame cupped against the wind, and did not turn my head when, from behind one of those doors, there came the faintest sound: the brittle fracture of dry toast between teeth.

Now I think of him often, though I never knew his name.

I imagine him seated at a narrow table, the plate before him bare except for crumbs. No butter, no jam, only the chalky bread and a cup growing cold in its saucer. His hands are clean, perhaps too clean. The room is not poor exactly, but reduced, like a sentence revised until only its grief remains. On the wall, a print hangs slightly crooked: a city piazza or a long arcade, lines fleeing toward a single invisible point. Once, he had studied such things—the obedient roads in paintings, the tiled floors that narrowed into distance, the tender deceit by which the world could be made to deepen on a flat surface.

Perspective: how everything diminishes as it leaves us. How the beloved face becomes a geometry of absence. How even a river, seen from a window in winter, gathers light not as water gathers it in summer—shattering and flinging it back—but slowly, solemnly, like someone collecting letters from the dead.

Perhaps he sits there each afternoon and watches the pale hours accumulate along the banks. The trees stand black and exact. The river does not speak, yet it has carried so much away that silence seems its only honest language. In that room, the man lifts the toast to his mouth and remembers vanishing points, remembers how masters made distance obey them, how arches and roads and windows could be arranged to lead the eye inward, inward, toward meaning.

And I—who might have knocked, who might have asked nothing more than may I come in—continued down the corridor, past all one hundred doors, toward whatever trivial brightness awaited me then.

What I regret is not that I lost him.

I regret that I never let him become real.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a highly stylized paragraph-poem imitating avant-garde fiction, full of long sentences, compressed syntax, art-historical imagery, private interiors, “nothingness,” and an ending with snowy roofs, wet trouser cuffs, a hill, and river light.
counterfactuals.output: In the room where the mirror had forgotten its duty and reflected only the pale intervals between objects, the chairs leaned inward like minor saints in a damaged fresco, the table held its bowl of black fruit with the severity of a Dutch interior, and all afternoon the wallpaper—green, flayed, botanical—seemed to breathe a thin museum-dust of extinguished conversations, while behind the curtain the city gathered itself into planes of zinc and pearl, a Cubist weather, a broken annunciation of windows, stairwells, hidden kitchens, the small ceremonial clatter of cups; I was there and not there, folded into the lacquered cabinet, into the blue vein of the porcelain vase, into the long sentence of the corridor where doors opened onto further doors and each threshold disclosed not revelation but nothingness, a furnished nothingness, embroidered, perfumed, with a bedspread white as a plaster cast and a lamp whose shade glowed like the inside of a throat; and because the afternoon had no center, because the clock dispersed its numbers like black birds over a winter field, I watched the paintings on the wall rearrange their dead—Venetian red, Sienese hand, gold leaf crumbling around the faces of impossible children—until even memory became an object in the room, small, handled, placed beside the ashtray, beside the letter never sent, beside the glove retaining the form of a vanished hand; then evening entered without argument, extinguishing the furniture one edge at a time, and I went out carrying the room inside me, its polished absences, its intimate catastrophes, into streets where the roofs were snowy, my trouser cuffs wet, and beyond the hill the river light kept opening and closing like a blade.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
